### **Introduction** 

In the previous lesson, you learned how to create a class diagram for a real-world system like a library management system. You probably identified classes such as Book, Student, and Librarian, listed their attributes (title, author, and due date), and defined their methods (borrow\_book() and return\_book()). Then, you translated the class diagram into functional code. Once you create a class and turn it into code, you probably wonder if anyone could directly change a book's number of copies to a negative number or accidentally change the student number. That would cause errors and confusion. This is where Encapsulation comes in. 

Encapsulation is one of the core principles of Object-Oriented Programming (OOP). It hides internal details of an object's properties and behavior from any external code. It also binds together all code related to the object's properties and behavior, controlling how it is accessed and modified. This prevents accidental changes to your data and hides the internal workings of your class.

Think of encapsulation like a capsule medicine 💊 — everything inside is protected and organized. In programming, we keep data safe inside a class and control how it is accessed.

This module will discuss Encapsulation, the principle of protecting the data inside a class and controlling how it is accessed or modified. It will present the way to manage data changes safely and correctly, rather than allowing direct access.

### 

### **Module Learning Objectives**

2. Explain how encapsulation protects data and improves code organization.

### **Key Concepts and Learning Activities** 

***1.1  Encapsulation with Functions***

Functions are a prime example of encapsulation because when you call a function, you generally don't care how it works internally. A well-written function contains a series of steps that make up a larger single task that you care about.  The name of the function should describe the name it embodies. 

The built-in len() function in the Python Standard Library returns the number of characters in a string or the number of elements in a list. You pass a string or list, and it returns the count.  When you write code that calls this function, you do not care about how the len() does it, or how many lines of code it contains, or whether it uses a local variable or a number of local variables. You just need to know what arguments to pass in and how the result is returned. 

The same is true for the functions that you write. Once you have tested the function and found that it works, you no longer worry about the details of its implementation. You only need to know which arguments to pass to the function and what it returns. 

	  
***1.2  What Encapsulation Is  in Object-Oriented Programming (OOP)***

In OOP, we keep data and code together in a class so everything that belongs together stays together. This makes our programs easier to understand and fix. If we use variables and functions anywhere, things can get messy and confusing. Classes help us organize our code, so we know where to find things and how they work.

Think of a TV remote control. The remote has buttons (data) and ways to use them (method). You don't need to know how the remote works inside; you just press the buttons to change the channel or volume. The remote keeps everything together and hides the details from you. That's like encapsulation—keeping things together and hiding the messy parts\!

Encapsulation is the process of bundling data (variables) and methods into a single unit called a class.

(image source: https\://www\.geeksforgeeks.org/python/encapsulation-in-python/)

It restricts direct access to the data and controls access through methods to protect the data within a class. Watch the following video that offers a visual explanation of encapsulation

***1.3** **public, protected, and private Modifiers*** 

Classes can have private, protected (hidden), and public (open) members. 

We need private members to keep important data safe. If persons with access to the code can change anything in a class, mistakes could happen, and things could break. Keeping some members private helps protect parts of the code that shouldn't be changed, so the code works the way we want it to. Identifying which parts of a class are private or public is done using access modifiers: **private, public, and protected**.  In Python, these are represented by symbols rather than keywords, as in other programming languages.

**Modifier	Symbol in Python		Meaning**  
private	 	double underscore  (\_\_) 	Accessible only inside the class  
protected 	single underscore  (\_)		Accessible within the same package   
public			none			Accessible anywhere

For encapsulation, attributes are usually ***private,*** and methods are usually ***public or protected.***

Let’s create a class **Student** with public attributes, name and age. 

| ![][image2]       Python:  class Student:     def \_\_init\_\_(self, name, age):         self.name \= name         self.age \= age |
| :---- |

	  
Since name and age are public members, they can be accessed anywhere. A person with access to the computer program might accidentally assign a negative value to age. If this happens, the program may have an invalid record and an inaccurate report. 

This problem can be avoided by setting the attribute as private. Private members of the class are accessible only inside the class. In Python, a double underscore '\_\_’ is placed before the identifier, which sets the attribute as private.   

|     Python: class Student:     def \_\_init\_\_(self, name, age):         self.\_\_name \= name         self.\_\_age \= 0         self.set\_age(age)      def set\_age(self, age):         if age \> 0:             self.\_\_age \= age  |
| :---- |

**Code explanation:** 

The code defines a class named **Student** with name and age attributes and uses encapsulation \- hiding data and controlling access to it.   

The **\_\_init\_\_( )**  method is the constructor in Python. It runs automatically when a new object is created. Creating a Student object requires two values: name and age, as defined in the constructor.  These values are assigned to the class variables name and age. 

Creating a student object :  	s1 \= Student(“Rizal” , 14\)

The double underscore in   **self.\_\_name**  and **self.\_\_age** makes name and age private attributes.  They cannot be accessed directly from outside the class; getting or changing their values must be done through special methods to ensure the data remains protected. 

Notice that a temporary value of 0 is assigned to age. This ensures a default value before validation. Then the method **set\_age()** is called to set the age correctly.  This method checks the value of age before assigning it to the variable. 

It is important to know when to use each access modifier in real-world projects. Proper use protects your code, improves readability, and enhances maintainability.  The following learning resource provides further explanation of Python's access modifiers.

**Learning resource 2**: [Access Modifiers in Python](https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/python/access-modifiers-in-python-public-private-and-protected/)

***1.4 Setter and Getter Methods*** 

Getters and setters are special methods that let you safely get or change private data.

A **setter** method updates (sets) the value of a private attribute. Usually, it contains a code that controls or validates the value to be stored in the private attribute.  

A **getter** method, on the other hand, retrieves (gets) the value of a private attribute.  We use getters to read private data and setters to change the private attributes.

Let's have the Student class again and enhance it by implementing setter and getter methods. 

![][image3]

This time we added setter methods, set\_name()  and set\_age(), and getter methods, get\_name() and get\_age(), to the class diagram.  See how they are added to the code.   
 

| Python: class Student:     def \_\_init\_\_(self, name, age):         self.\_\_name \= name         self.\_\_age \= 0         self.set\_age(age)     \#setter and getter methods for name     def set\_name(self, name):         self.\_\_name \= name     def get\_name(self):         return self.\_\_name     \#setter and getter methods for age     def set\_age(self, age):         if age \> 0:             self.\_\_age \= age     def get\_age(self):         return self.\_\_age  |
| :---- |
|  |

The setter methods are **set\_name()**  and **set\_age().** These methods allow you to update the name and age attributes of a student object, respectively. 

**set\_name()**  updates the name; it has no validation.

**set\_age()** updates the age only if the age is greater than 0\. If age is negative or zero, it will not change the value.  This is called data validation

The getter methods are **get\_name()** and **get\_name().** These methods return the student's name and age, respectively.

Let's create a Student object, s1,  and test the methods.

| Python:   s1 \= Student("Mary Grace", 14\)  \#Create a student object print(s1.get\_name())       \#access the student's name and age print(s1.get\_age())        \#and print the data s1.set\_name("Mary Grace Piattos")  \#update the student's name s1.set\_age(-100)           \#and student's age      print(s1.get\_name())       \#print the student's data print(s1.get\_age())        \#name and age    |
| ----- |
| **Code Output:  ![][image4]** |

The code does not allow direct access to or updates of the attributes: names and age, because they are set as private members.  It also protects the object from invalid data because the set\_age() method validates the data.

**Getters and setters** provide a formal way to get and set values in an object. They enforce a layer of protection that allows access to instance variables only if the class writer permits it. Getters and setters help protect attributes from being changed incorrectly. They also let you control how data is accessed or updated.

You can write cleaner and easier-to-read code by using getters and setters as attributes instead of methods. This means you do not need to use parentheses when you access them. The next learning resource will show you how.

### **Key takeaways** 

Encapsulation is an object-oriented programming concept that binds data (attributes)  and methods that operate on that data into a unit, such as a class. It hides internal data and requires access through methods, protecting it from unwanted changes.

Classes can have private and public members.  Access modifiers determine whether class variables and methods can be accessed only inside the class (private), within the same package (protected), or outside the class (public).  

In Python, the access modifiers are symbols placed before the attribute identifier:  double underscore “\_\_” for private,  single underscore “\_” for protected, and none for public. 

Setter and getter methods are special methods used to safely change (setter) or retrieve (getter) the value of a class's private variables.

The @property decorator is a special feature in Python that lets you access methods as if they were regular attributes, providing a cleaner, more intuitive interface.
